paper_metadata.title: Qudit-based scalable quantum algorithm for solving the integer programming problem

summary: The paper proposes a gate-based qudit–qubit algorithm for integer programming with theoretical complexity O(d^(n/2) + m·n²·log d + n/ε_QPE) compared to classical brute force O(d^n). A numerical simulation solves a non‑convex integer program with 5 variables (3^5=243 states) and 4 constraints, finding the optimal solution with cost 4 and estimated ≤19 repetitions to reach 0.99 success probability.

experiments.description: Gate-based qudit-qubit circuit algorithm for solving a general integer programming problem, including constraint satisfaction via distillation and Grover amplification, followed by QPE-based cost optimization; demonstrated on a 5-variable non-linear non-convex integer program.

algorithm.variant: Qudit-based scalable integer programming algorithm with constraint distillation, Grover amplitude amplification, and QPE-based cost maximization
algorithm.parameter_initialization: All qudits and qubits initialized in |0>; qudit register put into uniform superposition with d-dimensional Hadamard gates; QPE register initialized with Hadamards

problem_formulation.encoding_details: n d-dimensional qudits encode n integer variables directly; m qubits encode constraint satisfiability; l qubits store QPE phase; one ancilla qubit used for controlled rotation
problem_formulation.objective_function: Maximize polynomial cost function C(x) over integer variables subject to polynomial inequality constraints Ci < hi
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Constraint distillation function fi(Ci,hi)=2 floor(Ci/hi) entangles feasible states with |1> on the constraint qubit; Grover amplitude amplification post-selects the feasible subspace; final measurement on ancilla/QPE register biases toward optimal cost

problem_instance.description: Non-linear integer program with 5 variables, 4 non-convex constraints, and 3-valued integer domains; used as numerical demonstration of the algorithm

dataset_specification.description: No external dataset; hand-crafted benchmark IP instance

problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Numerical simulation of the circuit; comparison against branch-and-bound, brute force, and Google OR-Tools CP-SAT; success probability and repetition count analyzed; figure-based probability distributions reported

implementation_details.classical_solver: branch and bound; brute force; Google OR-Tools CP-SAT
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Classical preprocessing used to estimate cost-function bounds and repetition count; relaxed continuous problem used to compute Cub
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measurement outcomes decoded to integer assignments; constraint satisfaction checked classically; repeated runs used to boost success probability

speedup_claims.factor: exponential reduction; dn/2 improvement over brute force
speedup_claims.conditions: general polynomial integer programming problem; worst-case feasible region size 1; gate-based qudit-qubit algorithm
speedup_claims.caveats: Claim is asymptotic and based on leading-order complexity; practical performance depends on QPE precision and feasible-region size.

speedup_claims.factor: faster than best-known exact classical algorithm O((log n)^3 n) for the stated regime
speedup_claims.conditions: asymptotic comparison in the paper's complexity analysis
speedup_claims.caveats: No direct runtime benchmark against Reis-Rothvoss is shown; comparison is analytical only.

speedup_claims.factor: better scaling than approximate classical algorithms for non-linear IP
speedup_claims.baseline_method: LP+rounding and other approximate IP methods
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states approximate methods may fail on non-linear constraints; no direct benchmark on those methods is provided beyond the example problem.
This is a classical-vs-classical comparison; not a quantum speedup measurement.

speedup_claims.conditions: for the benchmark instance; based on reported runtime comparison
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper does not provide absolute runtimes, only a relative statement.

complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(d^n) brute force; best-known exact classical algorithm O((log n)^{3n}) as stated in paper
complexity_analysis.total_operations_quantum: Leading-order total time complexity O(m·n^2·log d + d^(n/2) + n·ϵ_QPE^-1)
complexity_analysis.total_operations_classical: Brute force O(d^n); best exact classical O((log n)^3 n)

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not quantified; advantage discussed asymptotically via O(d^n) vs O(d^(n/2)) scaling.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Requires scalable multi-qudit processors, qudit–qudit and qudit–qubit entangling gates, Grover amplification over dn search space, and QPE precision ε_QPE; the paper only simulates a 5-variable example with 3^5=243 states.
limiting_factors: Only noiseless numerical simulation; no hardware implementation
Algorithm dominated by Grover amplitude amplification with cost O(d^(n/2))
Large circuit depth implied by repeated Grover iterations and QPE
Requires scalable qudit hardware which is currently experimental
Advantage shown only as asymptotic complexity comparison, not empirical scaling

notes: num_qubits inferred from the numerical demonstration: 5 qudits + 4 constraint qubits + 1 ancilla qubit = 10 total qubits/register elements; the paper explicitly reports 5 qudits, 4 qubits for constraints, and 1 ancilla qubit.

hardware.type inferred as simulator_other because the paper presents a numerical implementation in Python and discusses potential real hardware only in outlook, with no specific QPU experiment reported.
circuit_depth not explicitly reported as a single depth number; only subroutine scaling and gate-count asymptotics are given, so it remains null.
Authors explicitly claim an exponential reduction in time complexity from O(d^n) to O(d^(n/2)) for integer programming but only provide a numerical simulation for a small toy instance (n=5, d=3).
No quantum hardware experiment is performed; implementation is a Python numerical simulation.
